data.name: France
data.summary: France taxes dividends, interest and gains on securities under the flat tax (PFU) of 31.4% from 2026 (12.8% income tax plus 18.6% social charges, up from 30%), plus the high-income surtax (CEHR, 3%-4%) and the differential contribution (CDHR) that lifts income tax on very high incomes to at least 20%, giving about 38.6% at the top. Real estate wealth above EUR 1.3 million bears the IFI (0.5%-1.5%); financial assets are not subject to wealth tax. Inheritance and gifts to children: EUR 100,000 allowance per child per parent, renewed every 15 years, then 5%-45% (45% above about EUR 1.9 million per child). The impatriate regime (art. 155 B CGI) exempts 50% of foreign passive income for eight years but requires taking up a job or business activity in France.

regimes.name: Ordinary tax residence
regimes.description: Residents (foyer, main abode, professional activity or centre of economic interests in France) are taxed on worldwide income; investment income under the PFU flat tax unless the household opts for the progressive scale for all such income.
regimes.eligibility: French tax domicile under art. 4 B CGI: home or main place of stay in France, main professional activity in France, or centre of economic interests in France. Non-EU citizens need a long-stay visa or residence permit.

capital_gains.summary: Gains on shares and bonds are taxed under the PFU at 12.8% income tax plus 18.6% social charges = 31.4% (the 18.6% rate applies to gains realised from 2025). Households with reference income above EUR 500,000 (couple) also pay the CEHR of 3% (4% above EUR 1 million), and the CDHR tops income tax up to an average of 20% of reference income above EUR 500,000 (couple), so a large gain of a wealthy household is taxed at about 38.6%. Real estate gains (other than the main home) are taxed at 19% plus 17.2% social charges, with taper relief giving full income tax exemption after 22 years and full social charge exemption after 30 years, plus a surtax of 2%-6% on gains above EUR 50,000.
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: No annual allowance for securities gains under the PFU. Main home exempt. Real estate: taper relief, exempt after 30 years. Holding-period allowances (50%/65%/85%) only for shares bought before 2018 and only under the progressive-scale option.
capital_gains.important_exceptions: Exit tax (art. 167 bis CGI) on leaving France after 6 of the last 10 years of residence, on unrealised gains on shareholdings of at least 50% of a company's profits or securities worth more than EUR 800,000 in total; deferred automatically for moves to the EU/treaty countries and cancelled after 2 years (5 years above EUR 2.57 million) if not sold (details from general knowledge, not re-read). Social charges on investment income are 7.5% only for people insured in another EEA state, Switzerland or the UK. CDHR confirmed for 2026 income: under art. 224 CGI as amended by the 2026 Finance Law (loi n° 2026-103, art. 2) it applies from 2025 income until the year in which the budget outturn shows a general government deficit below 3% of GDP (BOFiP ACTU-2026-00104, 30 June 2026).

capital_gains.rate_basis: PFU 12.8% income tax + 18.6% social charges = 31.4%; CEHR 4% (couple above EUR 1 million) brings income-tax-type levies to 16.8%, and CDHR raises income tax plus CEHR to an average of 20% of reference income, so 20% + 18.6% = 38.6% for a household whose income is mostly investment income. Real estate: 0 because held longer than 30 years (income tax exemption after 22 years, social charges after 30); earlier the rate is up to 19% + 17.2% + 6% surtax + CEHR. Foreign real estate: treaties usually give France the right to tax with a credit for situs tax; same taper.
capital_gains.professional_trader: Habitual securities trading by a private individual is rarely recharacterised as business income (BNC/BIC); the risk is mainly for real estate dealers (marchand de biens).
capital_gains.holding_period_rules: None for securities under the PFU. Real estate: taper from year 6, income tax exempt after 22 years, social charges after 30 years.
capital_gains.foreign_assets: Worldwide gains taxed; same rates for foreign securities.

dividends.summary: Dividends and interest, French or foreign, are taxed at the PFU of 31.4% from 2026 (12.8% income tax plus 18.6% social charges; 30% before), withheld as a prepayment for French-source income. High-income surtaxes CEHR (3%/4%) and CDHR (20% minimum average income tax) apply on top, giving about 38.6% at the top. Option for the progressive scale (with a 40% dividend allowance) for all investment income if more favourable.
dividends.important_exceptions: The 2026 Social Security Financing Law raised CSG on investment income by 1.4 points (social charges 17.2% to 18.6%); real estate income and gains, life insurance and regulated savings stay at 17.2%. Service-Public confirms social charges on investment income of 18.6% from 1 January 2026 and the PFU income tax part of 12.8%. CDHR applies to 2026 income (art. 224 CGI as amended by loi n° 2026-103, art. 2; BOFiP ACTU-2026-00104).

open_questions: Whether the treaty credit can also be imputed on the 18.6% social charges was not settled: art. 200 A imputes it on the flat-rate income tax, but the DGFiP notice 2047 describes the credit cap as income tax plus social charges. The 25.8% above assumes income tax only.
dividends.rate_basis: 12.8% + 18.6% = 31.4% PFU, plus CEHR/CDHR lifting income tax to an average of 20%: 20% + 18.6% = 38.6%. Foreign dividends: treaty withholding (typically 15%) is credited against French income tax, not against social charges. Treaty withholding on foreign dividends is imputed on the 12.8% flat income tax only (art. 200 A 1°, A: the tax withheld abroad is imputed on the flat-rate tax 'dans la limite du credit d'impot auquel il ouvre droit'), and conventional credits are added back to income tax in the CDHR formula (art. 224 IV A 2°), so with 15% withheld the credit absorbs 12.8 points, not 15: the French tax left on a foreign dividend is 20% + 18.6% - 12.8% = 25.8%, against 23.6% if the whole 15% were credited.
dividends.withholding_outbound: 12.8% on dividends paid to non-resident individuals (25% to non-resident companies, 75% to non-cooperative states), reduced by treaties; 0% to EU parent companies.
dividends.treaty_network: About 120 income tax treaties, one of the largest networks, including the US (count from general knowledge).
dividends.holding_company_notes: A French holding company pays 25% corporate tax; the participation exemption taxes only 5% (or 1% in a tax group) of dividends from holdings of at least 5%. A new tax on non-operating assets held in personal holding companies was debated in the 2026 budget; status not verified.

wealth_tax.summary: IFI (impôt sur la fortune immobilière) is levied on net real estate wealth (direct and indirect, including real estate held through companies and funds, not used for one's own business) when it exceeds EUR 1.3 million on 1 January; the scale then applies from EUR 800,000. Financial assets such as listed shares and bonds are not taxed. A 30% allowance applies to the value of the main home. New residents are exempt on foreign real estate for five years.
wealth_tax.exemptions_thresholds: Entry threshold EUR 1.3 million; brackets from EUR 800,000; decote between EUR 1.3 million and 1.4 million (EUR 17,500 minus 1.25% of the net value). 30% allowance on the main home (from general knowledge). Real estate used in the taxpayer's own business is exempt.
wealth_tax.eligibility_conditions: Residents: worldwide real estate (except during the newcomer period); non-residents: French real estate.
wealth_tax.important_exceptions: Proposals in the 2026 budget debate to turn IFI into a tax on 'unproductive wealth' and the 2% 'Zucman tax' on fortunes above EUR 100 million were not enacted as far as could be checked (PwC, reviewed April 2026, mentions no such change). New arrivals not resident in the previous five years are exempt on non-French real estate until 31 December of the fifth year after arrival.

components.name: IFI - real estate wealth tax
components.notes: Marginal scale on net taxable real estate value (art. 977 CGI as reported by Service-Public). Entry threshold EUR 1.3 million with decote up to EUR 1.4 million. Base includes real estate held indirectly through companies and funds.

wealth_tax.property_tax_note: Taxe foncière on all property owners and taxe d'habitation on second homes, set locally; separate from IFI.

inheritance.summary: Each child receives EUR 100,000 tax-free from each parent; gifts from the same parent in the previous 15 years use up the allowance. Above it, direct-line rates are 5% to 45% (marginal), with 45% above EUR 1,805,677 of taxable value per child. Worldwide assets are taxed if the deceased lived in France; spouses and PACS partners are exempt. Life insurance (assurance-vie) has a separate regime with an extra EUR 152,500 allowance per beneficiary for premiums paid before age 70.
inheritance.exemptions_thresholds: EUR 100,000 per child per parent (renewed after 15 years); extra EUR 159,325 for a disabled child. Cash gift exemption EUR 31,865 (donor under 80, adult child), renewable every 15 years, cumulative with the allowance.
inheritance.eligibility_conditions: Scope: worldwide assets if the deceased/donor is French-resident, or if the heir has been French-resident for at least 6 of the last 10 years; French assets always.
inheritance.important_exceptions: Dutreil pact: 75% exemption on qualifying operating businesses with collective and individual holding commitments; not for portfolios. Life insurance: 20%/31.25% after EUR 152,500 per beneficiary for premiums before 70 (art. 990 I CGI; from general knowledge).

open_questions: Life-insurance allowance (art. 990 I / 757 B) and Dutreil details were not re-read in the code; check for 2026 Finance Law changes to the Dutreil pact.
Notary fees on a succession (regulated emoluments, mandatory where real estate is involved) were not sourced; other_transfer_cost_rate set to 0.
inheritance.spouse_note: A surviving spouse or PACS partner is exempt from inheritance tax (CGI art. 796-0 bis; service-public.fr).
inheritance.gift_tax: Gifts use the same EUR 100,000 allowance and 5%-45% scale; the allowance renews every 15 years per parent and child. Plus a EUR 31,865 cash-gift exemption (donor under 80) renewable every 15 years. Gifts of bare ownership with retained usufruct are valued at a discount depending on the donor's age.
inheritance.business_relief: Dutreil pact (art. 787 B CGI): 75% of the value of shares in an operating company exempt with collective (2 years) and individual (4 years) holding commitments and a management role; does not apply to holding companies of listed portfolios.
inheritance.foreign_assets: Worldwide if the deceased/donor is resident, or the heir has been resident 6 of the last 10 years. Foreign inheritance tax on foreign assets credited (art. 784 A); estate tax treaties with about 35 countries including the US.
inheritance.domicile_rules: French domicile (art. 4 B) of the deceased/donor at the time of transfer makes worldwide assets taxable; there is no post-departure tail for the donor, but an heir resident 6 of the last 10 years pays French tax on foreign assets from a non-resident parent.

regimes.name: Impatriate regime (art. 155 B CGI)
regimes.description: For people recruited from abroad by a company in France, or who set up a business activity in France, after five years of non-residence: besides relief on employment income, 50% of foreign-source passive income (dividends, interest, gains on foreign securities, royalties) paid by companies in treaty countries with an administrative assistance clause is exempt from income tax, until 31 December of the eighth year after arrival. IFI and inheritance tax are unaffected (IFI already exempts foreign real estate for five years).
regimes.eligibility: Not French tax-domiciled during the five calendar years before the year of taking up the post; employee or listed corporate officer (e.g. SAS president, SA managing director) of a company established in France, recruited from abroad or moved within a group (BOI-RSA-GEO-40-10-10 §§ 10-150); must be French-domiciled through that professional activity. Someone whose only link with France is managing their own wealth is expressly excluded (§ 210). Non-salaried founders fall under a separate branch of art. 155 B that was not checked. The passive-income exemption is personal to the impatriate, not to other household members.

capital_gains.summary: 50% of gains on securities held abroad is exempt from income tax (art. 155 B II CGI); social charges of 18.6% are due on the full gain. Without high-income surtaxes that is 6.4% + 18.6% = 25%, but for a household with reference income above EUR 500,000 the CDHR tops income tax up to 20% of reference income, so the effective rate is about 28.6% (if the exempt half is left out of reference income) to 38.6% (if it is included).
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: 50% of qualifying foreign passive income and gains exempt from income tax, for the impatriate only (not the spouse's or children's holdings).
capital_gains.eligibility_conditions: As regime eligibility. The paying person (for gains: the custodian, or failing that the company whose shares are sold) must be established outside France in a state whose tax treaty with France has an administrative assistance clause (BOI-RSA-GEO-40-10-30-10 § 60). Income collected abroad still qualifies if later transferred to a French account (§ 100).
capital_gains.important_exceptions: Social charges are due on the unreduced amount (BOI-RSA-GEO-40-10-30 § 10). How the exempt half is treated for CEHR and CDHR (whether it counts in the revenu fiscal de référence) was not verified; the JSON uses the lower bound of 28.6% (CDHR applied, exempt half excluded).

open_questions: Resolved 2026-10-16: art. 224 II 3° CGI deducts the income exempt under art. 155 B from the CDHR base, so the exempt half does not count and the 28.6% lower bound is the right figure (art. 224 text on codes.droit.org, consolidated 2026-09-01). The CEHR base (art. 223 sexies, revenu fiscal de reference) was not checked for the same exclusion.
The branch of art. 155 B for non-salaried persons (founders bringing an exceptional economic contribution) was not checked.
capital_gains.rate_basis: Foreign listed securities: 12.8% income tax on 50% = 6.4%, raised by CDHR to 20% of reference income; if only the taxable half is in reference income that is 10% of the gain, plus 18.6% social charges on the full gain = 28.6% (lower bound). Without CDHR (household reference income below EUR 500,000) it would be 25.0%. Other items as standard.

dividends.summary: 50% of foreign dividends and interest is exempt from income tax; social charges 18.6% on the full amount. 25% without surtaxes; about 28.6% to 38.6% for a household above the CDHR threshold (see capital gains). French dividends taxed as standard.

regimes.name: Holding company subject to corporate tax (société holding à l'IS)
regimes.description: The family holds its portfolio through a French SAS or SARL subject to corporate income tax (IS). Gains and dividends on portfolio stakes (under 5%) are taxed at 25% IS inside the company instead of 31.4%-38.6% personally, and the 18.6% social charges are deferred until profits are paid out (PFU 31.4%). The long-term and parent-subsidiary exemptions only reach stakes of at least 5%, so the gain is a lower rate plus deferral, not an exemption. IFI is unchanged (holding shares count only for any real estate inside) and inheritance tax is unchanged: the children inherit the shares at the standard 5%-45% rates on net asset value (Dutreil relief excludes passive holdings), so wealth tax and inheritance inherit the standard regime.
regimes.eligibility: Any French resident can form an SAS/SARL (minimum capital EUR 1) and contribute the portfolio. Contributing appreciated securities is a disposal for the contributor unless the deferral of art. 150-0 B ter CGI applies (contribution to a company the contributor controls). The family home must stay outside the company because of the 2026 holding tax on sumptuary assets.
regimes.duration_note: A holding vehicle has no statutory time limit; it lasts as long as the family keeps it and stays resident, subject to changes in the law.

structure.entity: Société holding patrimoniale à l'IS (SAS or SARL)
structure.payout_notes: Dividends paid to resident individuals bear the PFU: 12.8% income tax + 18.6% social charges = 31.4% (2026 rate). CEHR (3%/4%) and the CDHR 20% minimum only apply above EUR 250,000 (single) / 500,000 (couple) of household reference income (art. 223 sexies and 224 CGI). Paying the family EUR 400,000 net needs a gross dividend of about EUR 583,000 (400,000 / (1 - 0.314)), which is EUR 83,000 over the couple's threshold: the CEHR at 3% on that excess adds about 0.4 point, and the CDHR is nil because of its decote (art. 224 V) and the EUR 12,500 plus EUR 1,500 per child that it allows. 31.4% is used as the rate at today's amounts. The thresholds are not indexed, so a payout that grows with prices drifts up towards 20% + 18.6% = 38.6%, which the flat rate does not capture. Repayment of contributed capital or of a shareholder current account (compte courant d'associé) is tax-free, so a family that sells or lends assets to the company can withdraw that balance first without tax; the app's flat rate does not model this.
structure.substance_and_anti_avoidance: No substance test for a domestic holding, but abuse of law (L64 LPF) and the 'mini abus de droit' (L64 A, mainly tax-motivated acts) apply. Apport-cession (art. 150-0 B ter CGI): the personal gain on shares contributed to a controlled holding is deferred; if the holding sells them within 3 years it must reinvest, after the 2026 Finance Law, 70% (was 60%) within 3 years (was 2) in qualifying economic activity held 5 years; a listed portfolio does not qualify. Holding tax (new art. 235 ter C CGI, loi n° 2026-103, financial years closing from 31 Dec 2026): 20% a year on the market value of sumptuary assets (vehicles, yachts, aircraft, jewellery, horses, wines, housing used by the shareholders) in companies with assets of at least EUR 5m and mainly passive income; listed securities and cash were removed from the base during the debates, so a pure portfolio holding is not taxed, but the home must not be held in it. 3.3% social contribution only on IS above EUR 763,000 (this family's IS is about EUR 450,000). CFC rules (art. 209 B) do not concern minority listed stakes.
structure.exit_and_liquidation: Shareholders who emigrate fall under the exit tax of art. 167 bis CGI if their securities exceed EUR 800,000 (or 50% of a company's profits): the unrealised gain on the holding shares is assessed, with automatic deferral for moves within the EU/EEA and cancellation after 2 years (5 years above EUR 2.57m) if still held (thresholds from general knowledge, not re-verified). On liquidation the company pays 25% IS on latent gains, then the liquidation surplus over contributed capital is taxed as a dividend (PFU 31.4%).

capital_gains.summary: Inside a holding at IS, gains on listed portfolio shares are ordinary profit taxed at 25%. The long-term regime (88% exempt, 12% quote-part taxed, i.e. 3% effective) only covers titres de participation, in practice stakes of at least 5% held at least 2 years, which a diversified listed portfolio never reaches. Social charges are not due inside the company; they are paid with the PFU when profits are distributed.
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: Long-term regime: titres de participation (including shares qualifying for the parent-subsidiary regime, at least 5%) held 2+ years: 88% exempt.
capital_gains.eligibility_conditions: Company must be subject to IS (SAS/SARL/SA, or an SCI that opted for IS).
capital_gains.important_exceptions: 2026 Finance Law: new 20% holding tax on sumptuary assets (not securities) from financial years closing 31 Dec 2026; apport-cession reinvestment raised to 70% within 3 years with a 5-year holding. Real estate inside a company gets no holding-period taper and is taxed at 25%.

open_questions: The 5%/2-year participation thresholds are taken from PwC; the art. 219 I a quinquies wording (titres de participation) was not re-read on Légifrance.
Exact final text of art. 235 ter C CGI (holding tax) not read on Légifrance; based on Deloitte's analysis of the adopted law.
capital_gains.rate_basis: IS standard rate 25%; the 3.3% social contribution only applies to IS above EUR 763,000 and is not reached. Private business sale: a stake of at least 5% held 2 years is a titre de participation, 12% quote-part x 25% = 3%. Local real estate held by the company: 25% of the gain, no taper (individuals are exempt after 22/30 years). Foreign real estate left null: depends on the treaty (often taxed in the situs state with a French credit). The 15% SME rate on the first EUR 42,500 is ignored (worth about EUR 4,000 at most).
capital_gains.professional_trader: Not relevant: all gains of an IS company are business profits at the same 25%.
capital_gains.holding_period_rules: No holding-period relief for portfolio shares; 2-year holding for the long-term regime on participations.
capital_gains.foreign_assets: Gains on foreign listed shares are taxable in France at 25%; treaties normally give France the sole right to tax them.

dividends.summary: Portfolio dividends (stakes under 5%) are fully taxable at 25% IS; the parent-subsidiary regime (95% exempt, 99% within a tax group) needs at least 5% of the capital held 2 years. Treaty withholding on foreign dividends (typically 15%) can be credited against IS, capped at the French tax on that income, so a 15% US withholding leaves 10% of French IS.

income.name: France

income_tax.summary: French income tax for 2026 (on 2025 income) is calculated per household share: 0% to EUR 11,600, 11% to EUR 29,579, 30% to EUR 84,577, 41% to EUR 181,917 and 45% above, with extra surtaxes of 3% above EUR 250,000 and 4% above EUR 500,000 for a single person (so 48% and 49%). Employees pay roughly 20.5% of gross pay in social contributions including CSG/CRDS; a micro-entrepreneur providing liberal services pays 25.6% of turnover.

employment_deduction.note: Automatic 10% deduction for employment expenses, capped at EUR 14,555 (minimum not modelled).

income_tax.self_employed_notes: Micro-entrepreneur (auto-entrepreneur) 2026: BNC (other services) 25.6% of turnover (was 24.6% in 2025), liberal professions under CIPAV 23.2%, BIC services 21.2%. Turnover ceiling EUR 77,700 for services; USD 60,000 is about EUR 52,000 so it stays under. The rate is on turnover, not profit. Above the ceiling the standard regime (TNS) applies, not modelled. VAT franchise threshold EUR 37,500 for services.
income_tax.local_tax_note: Single person, one share; a couple without children has two shares, which halves the income per share. Rates include the 3% and 4% high-income surtaxes (CEHR) per PwC; the minimum 20% high-income contribution (CDHR) is not modelled. No local income tax. Employee rate computed from the service-public.gouv.fr table valid 1 January 2026 (private-sector non-executive employee): below the social security ceiling (PASS EUR 4,005 a month, EUR 48,060 a year) old-age 6.90% + 0.40%, AGIRC-ARRCO tranche 1 3.15%, CEG 0.86%, CSG 9.2% + CRDS 0.5% on 98.25% of pay (= 9.53%) = 20.84%; above the ceiling (tranche 2 to EUR 32,040 a month) old-age 0.40% + AGIRC-ARRCO 8.64% + CEG 1.08% + CET 0.14% + CSG/CRDS 9.53% = 19.79%. Blended average: about 20.7% at EUR 54,000 and about 20.2% at EUR 130,000; 20.5% is used. Executives pay APEC 0.024% extra and no unemployment contribution is due. This replaces the earlier 22% taken from the low end of PwC's 22-25% range.

regimes.name: Impatriate regime (art. 155 B CGI)
regimes.description: Employees assigned to France by a foreign employer or recruited abroad, who were not French tax residents in the five calendar years before arrival, may exempt either their actual salary supplements linked to the move or a flat 30% of total remuneration (for positions taken up from 16 November 2018); pay for foreign workdays can also be exempt, with total exemptions capped at 50% of total remuneration (or at 20% of taxable remuneration for supplements plus foreign workdays). Taxable pay cannot fall below that of a similar job at a comparable French company.
regimes.duration_note: Eight years from the year of arrival.

succession.name: France
succession.summary: Children are guaranteed half, two thirds or three quarters of the estate, depending on how many there are. A foreign national resident can choose their national law, but French children can claim a compensatory levy on French assets if that law protects no one. Trusts are not part of French law but are taxed heavily; there is no private family foundation.
succession.reserved_share: Children: 1/2 with one child, 2/3 with two, 3/4 with three or more (Code civil art. 913). The spouse is protected at 1/4 only when there are no children (art. 914-1).
succession.foreign_law_note: Reg. 650/2012 art. 22 allows a choice of nationality law. But art. 913 para. 3 (Law 2021-1109 of 24 August 2021, for estates opened from 1 November 2021) lets children take a compensatory levy on French assets when the foreign law gives them no reserve, if the deceased or a child is an EU national or resident.
succession.trust_note: The fiducie (Code civil art. 2011 ff.) exists but cannot be used for gifts (art. 2013). France signed the Hague Trusts Convention in 1991 but the HCCH table shows no ratification or entry into force, so it is not in force. Foreign trusts are taxed under CGI art. 792-0 bis (trust reporting, 60 % gift and estate rate on certain transfers) and art. 990 J (annual 1.5 % levy on trust assets). Foundations are public-interest only (fondation reconnue d'utilite publique, fondation d'entreprise, fonds de dotation).
open_questions: Whether the Conseil constitutionnel or the Cour de cassation has ruled on the art. 913 compensatory levy was not found.
CGI article numbers for trust taxation are from memory and unchecked at legifrance.

assumptions: Top marginal rates: the real family's reference income (about EUR 1 million a year in dividends and realised gains) is above the EUR 660,000 at which the CDHR decote ends, so 20% of income is taken as the income-tax-type burden. The EUR 12,500 plus EUR 1,500 a child that the CDHR formula allows, and the PFU's lack of any allowance, are ignored (about 1.6 points of income at this level).

The art. 155 B impatriate regime is not a path: it needs the person to be recruited from abroad as an employee or corporate officer of a French company, and someone whose only link with France is managing their own wealth is excluded (BOI-RSA-GEO-40-10-10), so a family with no job cannot use it.
The portfolio's tax cost equals its value on arrival and is contributed to the holding at that value, so the contribution gives rise to no taxed or deferred gain (art. 150-0 B ter CGI).
At each death the whole estate passes to the three children with one EUR 100,000 allowance each; the first parent's allowance and the spouse exemption (art. 796-0 bis) are not modelled.

The IFI applies only to the EUR 5 million home; the portfolio is outside it. The social charges are the 18.6% rate for people affiliated to the French social security; the 7.5% rate for people insured elsewhere in the EEA is not used.
No lifetime gifts are modelled (the engine has deaths only).
open_questions: Needs an engine change: the payout tax of the holding depends on the size of the payout against thresholds that are not indexed (CEHR from EUR 500,000, CDHR 20% from EUR 660,000 for a couple, arts. 223 sexies and 224 CGI). A EUR 400,000 net payout needs about EUR 583,000 gross and bears about 31.8% at today's amounts; as prices rise the burden tends to 38.6%. The engine uses a flat 31.4%.

Needs an engine change: a life-insurance or capitalisation contract (assurance-vie, often a Luxembourg contract holding the portfolio) was considered and not modelled. Gains are taxed only on withdrawal, and at death the beneficiaries pay a levy of 20% (31.25% above EUR 700,000) after a EUR 152,500 allowance each for premiums paid before age 70 (art. 990 I CGI), instead of 5%-45% scale rates. The engine taxes income yearly and has no tax at withdrawal on the gain share, nor a per-beneficiary cap.

Needs an engine change: gifts. The EUR 100,000 allowance per child and parent renews every 15 years and gifts of bare ownership are valued at a discount, so lifetime gifts are the main French planning tool; the engine only models deaths.

Needs an engine change: the cotisation subsidiaire maladie (CSM) of up to 6.5% on investment income above 50% of the social security ceiling (EUR 24,030 for 2026), the base capped at 8 ceilings (EUR 384,480), would cost up to EUR 23,429 per adult a year if the family is affiliated to the French health system without earned income. The figures come from third-party simulators for 2026 (Indy); art. L380-2 of the social security code was not opened.

A foreign or French family trust was rejected: French law taxes the transfer of trust assets at death at the top rate of table III of art. 777 CGI (60%) when the settlor was French-resident (art. 792-0 bis II 2). A French family foundation does not exist (fonds de dotation and fondations are for public-interest purposes).

The holding tax of art. 235 ter C CGI is read from Deloitte and other summaries (listed securities not in its base); the promulgated text was not opened. Contributing an appreciated portfolio to a controlled holding defers the gain (art. 150-0 B ter), but a sale within three years requires reinvesting 70% in an economic activity; a listed-portfolio holding that trades would end the deferral. The recipe avoids this by assuming no gain at arrival.

Citations not opened: BOI-RSA-GEO-40-10-10 (read through the tax file only); Legifrance pages (403), so the consolidated CGI text from codes.droit.org was read instead; art. 219 I a quinquies and the treaty credit at corporate level were taken from summaries; the Deloitte, Meilleurtaux and Indy pages were seen only as search results, not opened; the Notice 2047 was opened but its passage on the credit cap is ambiguous.

CDHR (art. 224 CGI): the checks assume the 20% minimum average rate binds (38.6% with social charges). At about EUR 600,000 of income its smoothing and family allowance may leave it nil (31.4%, plus CEHR); above that range it binds. BOI-IR-CDHR-10 was not read.

Cotisation subsidiaire maladie: 6.5% on capital income above 50% of PASS when earned income is under 20% of PASS, base capped at 8 PASS (up to about EUR 23,400 a year), sourced only to calculator sites; whether it is per adult and applies to new residents insured through residence is unconfirmed. Not in the tax file or the projection.

paths.name: Holding the portfolio personally
paths.note: Dividends and gains bear the PFU: 12.8% income tax plus 18.6% social charges (from 1 January 2026). At the family's income the high-income contributions lift income tax to a 20% average (CEHR and CDHR, art. 223 sexies and 224 CGI), so 38.6% in all. IFI taxes the real estate only (not the portfolio). Inheritance tax is charged per child after a EUR 100,000 allowance, 5% to 45%; the portfolio is in the estate and unrealised gains are not taxed at death.

paths.name: Holding company subject to corporate tax (holding a l'IS)
paths.regime: Holding company subject to corporate tax (société holding à l'IS)
paths.note: A French SAS or SARL owned by the parents holds the portfolio. It pays 25% corporate tax on dividends and gains (no participation exemption below a 5% stake), with the treaty withholding credited, and a running cost; payouts to the parents bear the PFU. The shares are in the estate at market value (the Dutreil pact does not cover a passive holding), so inheritance tax is the same as for personal holding. The 2026 holding tax on sumptuary assets (art. 235 ter C CGI) does not reach listed securities, provided the home stays outside the company.

immigration.name: France
immigration.summary: EU citizens need no permit. Non-EU nationals have a talent passport for economic investors (at least EUR 300,000 in fixed assets and 30% of the capital of a company, creating or keeping jobs), a long-stay 'visiteur' permit for people living on their own means without working, and the usual employer-sponsored permits. There is no digital nomad visa and no citizenship by investment.
immigration.naturalisation: Five years of regular residence (two with a French higher-education degree or services to France); French at B2 and a civic knowledge test since 1 January 2026; discretionary decision by the Ministry of the Interior.
immigration.dual_citizenship_note: France does not require renunciation (general knowledge; the service-public pages retrieved did not state it).
